clue.text: Dot put duck in drink after slug

indicators.note: the slug comes after the rest in the clue but stands first in the answer

parts.note: a slug is a bullet fired from a gun

indicators.note: the duck is put somewhere, the first half of the instruction to place it inside
says where the duck goes: into the drink

parts.note: a pint is a drink of beer
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, so O

explanation.surface: A cryptic recipe: a drinker drops a duck into a pint after knocking back a slug of spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slug' looks like a swig of liquor, but here it is the bullet. 'Put ... in' sets O inside PINT to make POINT.
explanation.definitionFit: A dot marking each item in a list is called by this typographical name.

clue.text: Male lover's dressed with type of bikini top

indicators.note: the lover is dressed with the other word, so it wraps around it like clothing

parts.note: a beau is a male lover; the 's stands for is
and means with, joining things together

explanation.surface: A boyfriend is decked out in a piece of swimwear.
explanation.definitionFit: A strapless strip of fabric worn across the bust is a style of bikini top with this French name.

clue.text: Airline's fate

definitions.meaning: the Polish national airline carries this name; the 's is a link word for is
one's fate is one's portion or destiny in life

explanation.definitionFit: LOT is the Polish flag carrier, and one's lot is one's fate or portion in life.

clue.text: Something fragrant eaten up by lunchtime, lemony

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters are read from the bottom, backwards
the answer is eaten by, swallowed inside, the words lunchtime and lemony

explanation.surface: Something with a lovely smell gets gobbled up at lunch and tastes of lemon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eaten' finds IMELE across lunchtIME LEmony, and 'up' turns it around.
explanation.definitionFit: Elemi is an aromatic resin from tropical trees, used in perfumes and incense.

clue.text: Back entrance in Bill Clinton's bottom

parts.note: a bill is a poster stuck on a wall

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about a back way in and a former US president's rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill Clinton' reads as one name; split it into the poster and the last letter of Clinton.
explanation.definitionFit: A postern is a small rear or side gate in a castle or city wall.

clue.text: Sweet thing hard to ignore in Chinese book

indicators.note: the hard letter is to be ignored, so it is left out of the book's name

parts.note: the I Ching is the ancient Chinese Book of Changes
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A dessert is so tempting it is hard to ignore in a Chinese book.
explanation.definitionFit: The sugary coating on a cake is a sweet thing in the most literal sense.

clue.text: One unlikely to give a little time, God's heading off

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time, a little of it

indicators.note: the head, the first letter, comes off the word for God

parts.note: God is called the Maker, the creator; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: Someone stingy with even a little time, while God is departing.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who only takes is the opposite of a giver, so is unlikely to give.

clue.text: See 25
Lowry's subject for one of 13's stories

definitions.meaning: L. S. Lowry painted thin, simplified figures of northern mill workers
13 is the children's author whose picture books include one about a figure made of a twig

explanation.definitionFit: Lowry's crowds are thin figures drawn like a child's sketch, and this is also a Donaldson picture book about a wooden father.

clue.text: Colleague of Buzz A and Michael C up for being in outer space?

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters are read from the bottom, backwards

parts.words: Colleague of Buzz A and Michael C
parts.note: Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins flew Apollo 11 with Neil Armstrong, named here in the same style as Neil A

explanation.surface: Asks whether the moonwalkers' crewmate was up for a trip to space.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the astronauts by first name and initial, so the colleague is NEIL A; read upwards it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An extraterrestrial creature is the classic being from outer space; the question mark flags the playful definition.

clue.text: Besides which, I do like to be singing about Tottenham's first reserve

indicators.note: the song's word goes about, around, the letter from Tottenham

parts.words: Besides which, I do like to be singing
parts.note: the music hall song I Do Like to Be Beside the Seaside: what is sung beside the word beside is the seaside

indicators.note: the first letter of Tottenham is taken

explanation.surface: A Spurs fan singing an old seaside song while their club's first reserve waits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I Do Like to Be Beside the Seaside' is a British music hall song; the word sung after 'beside' is SEASIDE. Tottenham is a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: To reserve something is to keep it apart for later use, a two-word phrasal verb.

clue.text: Could I be fit for friend?

parts.note: asking could I be turns into the question am I
go means in working order or ready, as in all systems go

explanation.surface: Someone wonders if they are fit enough to be a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is the Spanish word for a friend, used casually in English too.

clue.text: Finally roaming free in Cameroon, retiring animal of the desert

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: French is spoken in Cameroon, where free is libre

indicators.note: takes the final letter of roaming

explanation.surface: A shy creature roams free across Cameroon before retreating into its desert home.
explanation.definitionFit: The small burrowing rodent kept as a pet lives wild in the deserts of Africa and Asia.

clue.text: Granny clasping back in fall, silly sod, after trouble doing a backflip in sport, she writes

indicators.note: the granny part comes after the sport part
places the flipped word inside the sport

parts.note: judo is a martial art and sport

indicators.note: the word for trouble flips backwards

parts.note: to ail is to trouble, as illness does

indicators.note: granny clasps, holds inside her, the other letters

parts.note: nan is a British word for granny

indicators.note: the back letter in fall, its last
silly means the letters of sod are muddled

explanation.surface: Granny takes a tumble mid-backflip during judo, a silly old sod, all from a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The long surface hides a two-part charade; 'back in fall' means the back letter in fall, not a seasonal autumn. Nan is British for granny.
explanation.definitionFit: The British author of many bestselling rhyming picture books is a woman who writes.

clue.text: Couple upside-down in boudoir

indicators.note: in a down clue upside-down means read from the bottom, backwards
the letters sit inside the word boudoir

explanation.surface: A pair caught upside-down in the bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' finds OUD inside bOUDoir; 'upside-down' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people performing or acting together make a pair, a synonym for a couple.

clue.text: Story claimed to miss the odd parts

indicators.note: skipping the odd-numbered letters of claimed keeps the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: A claimed story that leaves out the strange bits.
explanation.definitionFit: A story told to deceive, a fib, is an untruth.

clue.text: Father Brown's ultimate temptress

parts.note: to sire is to father; a sire is a father

indicators.note: the ultimate letter of Brown is its last

explanation.surface: G. K. Chesterton's priest-detective Father Brown meets the ultimate seductress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father Brown' looks like Chesterton's sleuth, but splits into a father and Brown's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Sirens lured sailors with song, so a seductive woman takes their name.

clue.text: A few weeks to live in retreat among native Australians and Maoris, primarily, in one of 13's stories

indicators.note: the month and reversed verb go among, between, the two roos

parts.note: kangaroos, roos, are native Australians; two of them give the plural
a month is a few weeks

indicators.note: retreating, the word for living goes backwards

parts.note: to be is to live or exist

indicators.note: takes the primary, first, letter of Maoris

explanation.surface: A month to live, retreating among Aboriginal Australians and Maoris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native Australians' looks like people, but here means kangaroos, and the plural supplies two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: This Donaldson picture book tells of a witch whose flying vehicle has space for more passengers.

clue.text: Approximate location of misdirected golf ball?

definitions.meaning: an approximate figure is a ballpark estimate
a wayward shot lands in the long grass beside the fairway

explanation.definitionFit: A rough estimate is approximate, and the rough is the long grass where stray golf shots end up.

clue.text: Cat retracting tail a little in one of 13's stories

indicators.note: the tail, the final letter of the cat's name, is drawn back a little: moved one place earlier in the alphabet

parts.note: Tiddles is a stock British pet name for a cat

explanation.surface: A cat draws its tail in a little, in a children's story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retracting tail a little' is unusual: the last letter S is not removed but pulled back one step in the alphabet, becoming R. Tiddles is a typical British name for a pet cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Donaldson's picture book is about a small fish who tells tall tales, a tiddler being a tiny fish.

clue.text: Exceptional starter covered by newspaper — nothing that adds flavour?

indicators.note: the first letter is covered by, held inside, the newspaper

parts.note: a newspaper is an organ, a publication that speaks for a group

indicators.note: the starter of exceptional is its first letter

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: An exceptional first course is wrapped in newspaper, but adds no flavour?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covered by' places E inside ORGAN, the newspaper; the question mark marks a definition by description.
explanation.definitionFit: The dried leaves of wild marjoram are a herb added to Italian and Greek dishes for flavour.

clue.text: English town beginning to lose in board game, win less popular

indicators.note: puts that letter inside the board game

parts.note: ludo is a board game played with dice and counters

indicators.note: the beginning of lose is its first letter
the word for popular is taken away from win

parts.note: in means popular, fashionable

explanation.surface: Someone starts losing at a board game, and a win becomes less popular.
explanation.walkthrough: LUDLOW is a market town in Shropshire, England; 'less' removes IN from WIN, leaving W.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a historic market town in Shropshire, in the English West Midlands.

clue.text: Sound tip for music writer

indicators.note: says the word for tip is heard, matching the name

parts.note: to tip is to lean over, to list as a ship does

explanation.surface: A sensible piece of advice for someone who writes music.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt, the Hungarian Romantic pianist, was a composer of music.

clue.text: See 25
Vessel having to slow to a trot, might you say?

definitions.meaning: a glass container for serving wine or port

definitions.text: to slow to a trot, might you say?
definitions.meaning: a horse slowing from a canter to a trot is coming out of the canter, which might jokingly be named this

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is playful: a rider who drops from a canter to a trot de-canters, so the word fits as a whimsical coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoppered glass bottle holding wine or spirits is a vessel, and the joke reads it as un-cantering.

clue.text: Main, one fed to cook

indicators.note: the numeral is fed into the cook, going inside

parts.note: a chef is a cook
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The main meal is one fed to the cook.
explanation.definitionFit: Chief means principal or most important, the same as main in 'the main reason'.

clue.text: One of 13's stories, when she grapples with Thailand in fable

indicators.note: puts the jumble inside the tale

parts.note: a fable is a tale

indicators.note: the words wrestle with one another, so their letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: An author wrestles with Thailand in her fable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' looks like it points to 13, the author, but here it is only anagram fodder; the fable's word is split around the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: This Donaldson picture book follows a small mollusc who rides the ocean on the tail of a giant sea mammal.

clue.text: Kind of newspaper, pale back always

parts.note: i is a British newspaper

indicators.note: the word for pale goes back, reversed

parts.note: wan means pale
ay is an old poetic word for always

explanation.surface: A sort of newspaper that always has a pale back page.
explanation.walkthrough: The i is a British national daily newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means to some extent, as 'kind of' does in casual speech.

clue.text: In Turkey, an official story needing no introduction

indicators.note: the story loses its introduction, its first letter

parts.note: a saga is a long story

explanation.surface: A Turkish dignitary whose story needs no introduction.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Ottoman Empire an aga was a military commander or high official.

clue.text: One of 13's stories, where claw almost seizes male husky

indicators.note: the shortened claw seizes, wraps around, the other letters
almost the whole word, its last letter lopped

parts.note: a talon is a claw
he is a male
a husky voice is gruff

explanation.surface: A claw almost grabs a gruff husky male, as in a monster story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops N from TALON, leaving TALO, which 'seizes' HE and GRUFF.
explanation.definitionFit: Donaldson's best-known picture book features a monster invented by a mouse with claws and terrible tusks.
